lesson.title: How mass sets a star's life

steps.headline: A star's life is its fuel divided by its burn rate, and mass raises the burn rate faster than the fuel.

lead.text: On the main sequence a star fuses hydrogen in its core. Fuel grows roughly in proportion to the mass M. The burn rate, the luminosity, grows roughly as M³·⁵. Lifetime is fuel ÷ burn rate, so t ∝ M⁻²·⁵. The Sun lasts about 10 billion years.

steps.headline: Find the main-sequence lifetime of a 2 M☉ star.

workedSteps.text: Work out the power of the mass.
Divide the Sun's lifetime by it.

lead.text: Same rule, a heavier star. Give the answer in millions of years.

reveal.text: A star four times the Sun's mass lasts only about 3% as long. More fuel does not make up for a much faster burn.

lead.text: Turn the rule round. Divide the lifetime by 10 billion years to get M⁻²·⁵, then raise that number to the power −1/2.5 to get M.

reveal.text: A star that lasts only 10 million years is about 16 times the Sun's mass. Short lives mean heavy stars.

lead.text: The rule L ∝ M³·⁵ is a fit to measured main-sequence stars, good to about a factor of two. Split the power as 2³ × 2⁰·⁵.

reveal.text: A 10 M☉ star shines at about 3,200 L☉. Mass fixes where a main-sequence star sits on the H–R diagram.

lead.text: When core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and the outer layers swell into a giant. OpenStax's table of end states: below about 10 M☉ a white dwarf, from about 10 to 40 M☉ a neutron star, above that a black hole.

reveal.text: A star's initial mass decides its remnant. A 15 M☉ star sits in the middle band: its core collapses in a supernova but stops short of a black hole.

lesson.orientation: Estimate main-sequence lifetimes from mass and predict how a star ends.
lesson.reviewLabel: How mass sets a star's life
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A heavy star has more hydrogen fuel than a light one, but burns it far faster. Take star X, with 3 times the fuel of star Y, burning it 12 times as fast.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate how long a star shines from its mass, and what it leaves behind.

recap.keyIdea: A star's life is fuel divided by burn rate. Mass raises the burn rate faster than the fuel, so t ∝ M⁻²·⁵: heavy stars live short lives, and mass also decides the remnant.

blocks.text: You found that a 4 M☉ star lasts only 312.5 million years, that a star lasting 10 million years has about 16 times the Sun's mass, and that a 15 M☉ star leaves a neutron star.

recap.nextHook: Stars live and die inside galaxies. What does the light of distant galaxies tell us about the universe?

questions.prompt: Main-sequence lifetime scales as t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, with M in solar masses. Find the lifetime of a 4 M☉ star in millions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: Raise 4 to the power −2.5.
4²·⁵ is 4² × √4.
Divide 10 billion years by 4²·⁵ and convert to millions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4⁻²·⁵ = 1/32, so t = 10 billion/32 = 0.3125 billion years = 312.5 million years.

questions.onCorrect: 312.5 million years. 4²·⁵ = 32, so the lifetime is a thirty-second of the Sun's.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in billions of years. Convert to millions.
That divides by M alone. The burn rate rises with mass too, so divide by M²·⁵.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence luminosity scales roughly as L ∝ M³·⁵. How many times the Sun's luminosity does a 2 M☉ star have? Give one decimal place.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 2³·⁵ into 2³ × 2⁰·⁵.
Multiply 8 by √2.
questions.onCorrect: 11.3 L☉. 2³·⁵ = 2³ × √2: the exponent 3.5 is a power, not a multiplier.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the power 3 only. The exponent is 3.5, which adds a square root of 2.
That multiplies 2 by 3.5. The exponent is a power, so 2 is raised to it.

questions.prompt: Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find the main-sequence lifetime of a 0.5 M☉ red dwarf in billions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: A negative power of one half is a positive power of two.
Work out 2²·⁵.
Multiply by 10 billion years.
questions.onCorrect: 56.6 billion years. A negative power flips 0.5 to 2, so the lifetime grows.

misconceptions.feedback: That raises 0.5 to +2.5. The power is negative, which flips it to 2²·⁵.

questions.prompt: Following the OpenStax table of stellar end states, what remnant does a star of initial mass 15 M☉ leave? Answer in two words.
hints: Its core collapses in a supernova but stops short of a black hole.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A neutron star. Stars of about 10 to 40 M☉ end in a core-collapse supernova that leaves a neutron star.

questions.onCorrect: A neutron star. Stars of about 10 to 40 M☉ end in a core-collapse supernova.

misconceptions.feedback: Black holes need still heavier stars. At 15 M☉ the core collapses but stops short.
White dwarfs come from stars below about 10 M☉. This star is heavier.

questions.prompt: A star spends 10 million years on the main sequence. Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find its mass in solar masses, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Divide the lifetime by 10 billion years to get M⁻²·⁵.
Invert to get M²·⁵.
Raise 1,000 to the power 1/2.5.
questions.onCorrect: 16 M☉. Invert the rule: M is t ÷ 10 billion years raised to the power −1/2.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is M²·⁵. Raise it to the power 1/2.5 to get M.
That divides by 2.5. A power of 1/2.5 is a root, not a division.

questions.prompt: What will the Sun become after its red-giant stage?
hints: Compare the Sun's mass with the boundary for a supernova.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At 1 M☉ the Sun is well below the 10 M☉ boundary. It will shed its outer layers and leave a carbon-oxygen white dwarf about the size of Earth.

questions.onCorrect: A white dwarf. The Sun is well below the 10 M☉ boundary, so it sheds its outer layers.

misconceptions.feedback: Neutron stars come from stars of about 10 to 40 M☉. The Sun is far lighter.
Black holes need still heavier stars. The Sun is well below the boundary.

questions.prompt: How long does X's fuel last compared with Y's? Give a decimal.
hints: Lasting time is fuel divided by burn rate.
Take Y's fuel and rate as 1, so X's are 3 and 12.
Divide 3 by 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lifetime = fuel ÷ burn rate = 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 of Y's.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. X has more fuel, but it burns so much faster that the fuel lasts a quarter as long.

misconceptions.feedback: That is upside down. More fuel lengthens the life and a faster burn shortens it.
That multiplies fuel and rate. Fuel lengthens the time and burn rate shortens it, so divide.

questions.prompt: A star has more mass than the Sun. How does its main-sequence life compare?
hints: Compare how fast fuel and burn rate grow with mass.
questions.onCorrect: Burn rate grows much faster than fuel, so heavier stars live shorter lives.

misconceptions.feedback: More fuel, yes, but the burn rate grows far faster. The burn rate wins.
Burn rate depends strongly on mass, so lifetimes differ.

questions.prompt: Why is the exponent in M⁻²·⁵ negative?
hints: Divide M by M³·⁵.

acceptedIdeas: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.

choices.label: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
Mass is measured in solar units.

questions.onCorrect: M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵: the burn rate outgrows the fuel, so the lifetime shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign has nothing to do with size. It comes from dividing M by M³·⁵.
Solar units set the scale, not the sign of the exponent.

questions.prompt: Using L ∝ M³·⁵, how many times the Sun's luminosity does a 10 M☉ main-sequence star have? Give the nearest hundred.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 10³·⁵ into 10³ × 10⁰·⁵.
Multiply 1,000 by √10, then round to the nearest hundred.
questions.onCorrect: 3,200 L☉. A tenfold mass gives thousands of times the light.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 10 by 3.5. The exponent is a power applied to 10.
That is 10³. The exponent is 3.5, which adds a square root of 10.
